title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 226
paragraphs: In the land of Arabia, not far from Egypt, there is a gulf of the sea running in from what is called the Erythraean Sea — very long and narrow, as I am about to describe. As to the length of the voyage along it, a man setting out from the innermost point to sail through it into the open sea would spend forty days on the journey under oars; and as to its breadth, at its widest the gulf is half a day's sail across. It has an ebb and flow of tide every day. My view is that Egypt was once just such another gulf: the one running in towards Ethiopia from the Northern Sea, and the other, the Arabian gulf I am about to describe, running from the south towards Syria, the two gulfs boring in so as almost to meet at their far points, and passing one another with only a small space left between. Now if the stream of the Nile were to turn aside into this Arabian gulf, what would prevent that gulf from being filled up with silt as the river continued to flow — certainly within twenty thousand years? For my part I am of the opinion it would be filled up even within ten thousand. How then, in all the time that has elapsed before my birth, should not a gulf even much greater than this have been filled up by a river so great and so active?
